syllabus_version.title: CBSE Curriculum for the Academic Year 2026-27

topics.title: Introduction: the short story as a form

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the basic elements of a short story: plot, point of view and mode.
Distinguish the story of incident, the story of character and a story that works through form.
Explain how the short story differs from the novel in magnitude and economy.

topics.title: The opening: Iona and his horse in the twilight snow

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret how the snowy twilight setting prepares the reader for Iona's grief.
Explain the images used to describe the motionless Iona and his little horse.

topics.title: Iona's fares: the officer and the three young men

concepts.learning_objective: Analyse how the officer and the three young men respond to Iona's grief.
Describe Iona's repeated attempts to tell his passengers about his son's death.

topics.title: Alone with grief: the street, the stable and the horse

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the narrator's description of Iona's immense grief that no one notices.
Evaluate the significance of Iona finally telling his story to his horse.

topics.title: Chekhov, theme and language of the story

concepts.learning_objective: State facts about Chekhov and the theme of failed human communication in his stories.
Interpret words and expressions from the story, such as 'as if he were on needles' and 'snuffle'.

topics.title: Mustachios as markers of class

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the moustache styles the narrator links to different social classes.
Explain how the opening ridicules class pride and rigid social conventions.

topics.title: Seth Ramanand and Khan Azam Khan

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the moneylender Ramanand's nature as revealed by his words and actions.
Describe Khan Azam Khan's pride, poverty and headstrong nature.

topics.title: The quarrel over the moustache tips

concepts.learning_objective: Identify instances that show Ramanand's shrewd business sense.
Trace how each bargain costs Azam Khan more of his possessions.

topics.title: The ending: irony and message

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the irony of the story's ending.
Evaluate the author's message about false pride and social snobbery.

topics.title: Author, vocabulary and language

concepts.learning_objective: Recall key facts about Mulk Raj Anand and his writing.
Infer the meaning of expressions such as nouveau riche and goods and chattels from context.
Use phrases such as draw up a deed and keep one's word correctly.

topics.title: The whispering house

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the mother's inability to love and the family's social pretensions.
Explain how the unspoken demand for money haunts the house and the children.

topics.title: Luck and lucre

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the mother's idea of luck and how it differs from money.
Analyse why Paul sets out to prove that he is lucky.

topics.title: The rocking-horse and Bassett

concepts.learning_objective: Describe Paul's frenzied rides on the rocking-horse in search of luck.
Explain the secret betting partnership between Paul and Bassett.

topics.title: Winning at the Lincoln and the Leger

concepts.learning_objective: Recall how Paul's tip on Daffodil convinces Uncle Oscar.
Calculate winnings from the odds and stakes mentioned in the story.
Interpret Paul's claim that he wins only when he is 'sure'.

topics.title: The birthday gift and the louder voices

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the plan to give the mother money secretly and her response to it.
Analyse why the voices in the house grow louder after the money arrives.

topics.title: The Derby, Malabar and Paul's death

concepts.learning_objective: Recall the events leading to Paul's collapse and the Derby win.
Evaluate the irony of the ending and the symbolism of the rocking-horse.

topics.title: Language work: phrases and vocabulary

concepts.learning_objective: Explain idioms and phrases such as 'sure as eggs', 'spinning yarns' and 'turned to dust'.
Identify the meanings of words for facial expressions and other words from the story.

chapters.title: The Adventure of the Three Garridebs

topics.title: The narrator, the date and John Garrideb's arrival

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the narrator and explain how the opening frames the story and fixes its date.
Explain how Holmes reads the visitor's English outfit and Watson's directory search.

topics.title: John Garrideb's tale of the strange will

concepts.learning_objective: Recall the terms of Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's will as told by John Garrideb.
Analyse how Holmes tests and exposes the falsehoods in the visitor's story.

topics.title: Nathan Garrideb's museum and the Birmingham advertisement

concepts.learning_objective: Describe Nathan Garrideb's appearance, collection and dreams.
Interpret the American clues in the Howard Garrideb advertisement and the plan behind it.

topics.title: Holmes identifies Killer Evans and the Presbury link

concepts.learning_objective: Recall what Holmes learns about Killer Evans from the Scotland Yard records.
Explain how Holmes connects Rodger Presbury with Nathan Garrideb's room.

topics.title: The trap, the wound and the resolution

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the climax in the room and the secret hidden beneath the floor.
Evaluate what Watson's wound reveals about the friendship between Holmes and Watson.
Interpret the irony and subtle humour in the story's ending.

topics.title: Language: vocabulary and figurative expressions

concepts.learning_objective: Infer the meaning of difficult words and phrases from their context in the story.
Explain the figurative meaning of idiomatic expressions used in the story.

topics.title: Mammachi's pickle business and Pappachi's retirement

concepts.learning_objective: Recall how Mammachi's pickle and jam business began and grew.
Explain why Pappachi felt retirement as a humiliation and resented his wife's success.

topics.title: Cruelty at home, Chacko's intervention and the Plymouth

concepts.learning_objective: Describe Pappachi's violence and how Chacko put an end to it.
Interpret how Pappachi used his public image and the Plymouth to punish his family.

topics.title: The moth that was not named after him

concepts.learning_objective: Recall how Pappachi found the moth and what was first decided about it.
Analyse why the later reclassification became his life's greatest setback.

topics.title: Vienna, the violin and Pappachi's death

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why Mammachi's violin lessons in Vienna were abruptly stopped.
Interpret Ammu's comment on habit and the irony in the account of Pappachi's death.

topics.title: About the author and language work
topics.ncert_sections: About the Author; Language Work; Reading for the Blind

concepts.learning_objective: Identify Arundhati Roy and the novel from which the extract is taken.
Match kinds of scientists and kinds of writing with their meanings.
Interpret the account of how the Braille system developed from night writing.

topics.title: London years and the journey to America

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the narrator's frugal life among Bengali bachelors in London.
Explain why and how the narrator moved to America and what he learnt on the way.

topics.title: First weeks at the YMCA in Cambridge

concepts.learning_objective: Describe how the narrator adjusted to food, noise and routine at the YMCA.
Identify the differences between British and American usage and life that the narrator notices.

topics.title: Meeting Mrs Croft

concepts.learning_objective: Recall the narrator's first visit to Mrs Croft's house and the terms of his stay.
Interpret the details that build up the character of Mrs Croft.

topics.title: Mala and the narrator's family past

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the narrator's arranged marriage to Mala and his early indifference to her.
Explain how the memory of the narrator's mother shapes his response to Mrs Croft.

topics.title: Life in Mrs Croft's house and Helen's visits

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the evening ritual of the flag on the moon builds a bond between the narrator and Mrs Croft.
Analyse Helen's relationship with her mother and what it reveals about Mrs Croft.

topics.title: Mala's arrival and the narrator's reflection

concepts.learning_objective: Describe how Mala and the narrator begin their life together in America.
Explain why the visit to Mrs Croft becomes a turning point in the marriage.
Evaluate the narrator's closing reflection on his ordinary yet remarkable life on three continents.

topics.title: The train journey and Satyajit's ruin

concepts.learning_objective: Recall how the collapse of Satyajit's bank stripped him of his wealth and changed his outlook.
Interpret the recurring question 'What now?' as a sign of Satyajit's anxiety about the future.

topics.title: The forgerer and Satyajit's rise

concepts.learning_objective: Recall how Satyajit's detection of a forged cheque began his rise from clerk to accountant.
Evaluate the author's comment on crime, punishment and Satyajit's later change of feeling about the forgerer.

topics.title: Uncle Srinath's letter and the journey to Shantipur

concepts.learning_objective: Explain what Srinath means by 'benediction' and 'daughter crisis' in his letter.
Identify why Satyajit decides to attend the wedding at Shantipur.

topics.title: The welcome and the homage of the village

concepts.learning_objective: Describe how Srinath, his family and the villagers honour Satyajit on his arrival.
Analyse why Satyajit feels like an impostor while enjoying the 'twilight splendour of departed glory'.

topics.title: The dowry demand and the loss of house and pond

concepts.learning_objective: Analyse the irony of the cash dowry demand made of a man who has lost his fortune.
Interpret Satyajit's mortgaging of his house and pond and the story's closing image.

topics.title: Author, narration and language

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the author and explain how the story is narrated from Satyajit's perspective.
Interpret key expressions, sentence fragments and Indian idiom used in the story.

topics.title: The chance meeting and the invitation to Foyot's

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the story is framed as a flashback triggered by a meeting at the play twenty years later.
Describe the young narrator's poor circumstances and why flattery made him accept the luncheon.

topics.title: At the restaurant: salmon, caviare and Champagne

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the gap between the guest's claims about eating little and what she actually orders.
Explain how the narrator hides his alarm about money behind polite hospitality.

topics.title: The giant asparagus and the narrator's panic

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the narrator's growing panic as the guest orders the expensive asparagus.
Analyse the comic exaggeration and imagery used to describe the guest eating.

topics.title: Ice-cream, peaches and the bill

concepts.learning_objective: Recall how the peaches and the bill leave the narrator penniless for the month.
Interpret the narrator's parting retort and the guest's reply calling him a humorist.

topics.title: The ending: revenge, irony and humour

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the ironic 'revenge' in the final line, when the guest weighs twenty-one stone.
Identify instances of irony and self-mocking humour in the story.
Evaluate how the first-person narrative heightens the story's effects.

topics.title: The author and the language of the story

concepts.learning_objective: Recall key facts about William Somerset Maugham's life, works and style.
Infer the meanings of words such as mortifying, vindictive, complacency and ingratiating from context.

topics.title: Introduction: what poetry is

concepts.learning_objective: State the origin of the word 'poetry' and what it says about the poet and the poem.
Identify the characteristic features of poetry such as rhythm, metre and figures of speech.

topics.title: The peacock's sudden appearance and colours

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the colour images used to describe the peacock's neck and tail.
Explain how the poem shows the peacock as a bird glimpsed only briefly.

topics.title: Reading in the veranda: signs of the peacock

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the changes in the surroundings that signal the peacock is near.
Analyse the link the poem makes between deep absorption in a book and seeing the peacock.

topics.title: The tail that blinks: closing image, poet and vocabulary

concepts.learning_objective: Evaluate the closing image of the tail that blinks for eyes that are always open.
State facts about Sujata Bhatt and infer word meanings such as 'turquoise' and 'darts'.

chapters.title: Let Me Not to the Marriage of True Minds

topics.title: Love that does not alter (lines 1-4)

concepts.learning_objective: Explain what the speaker means by refusing to admit impediments to the marriage of true minds.
Interpret the claim that love which changes when circumstances change is not true love.

topics.title: The ever-fixed mark and the guiding star (lines 5-8)

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the image of love as an ever-fixed mark that looks on tempests unshaken.
Explain the metaphor of love as the star that guides every wandering ship (bark).

topics.title: Love and Time (lines 9-12)

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the poem shows love as independent of Time and physical beauty.
Interpret the image of Time's bending sickle and the special meaning of 'compass'.

topics.title: The closing couplet, the sonnet form and the poet
topics.ncert_sections: Lines 13-14; About the Poet; Try This Out

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret how the closing couplet stakes the poet's writing on the truth of his claim.
Identify the features of the Shakespearean sonnet and the poem's use of negatives.
Recall key facts about William Shakespeare and Sonnet 116.

topics.title: The evening light on the houses

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the image of 'light, chill and yellow' bathing the 'serene foreheads of houses'.
Identify personification in the opening lines and explain its effect.

topics.title: The thrush's song and the coming of spring

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the thrush's song announces spring and relates to the title 'Coming'.
Analyse the phrase 'fresh-peeled voice' and the idea of the song 'astonishing the brickwork'.

topics.title: The speaker's childhood and the child at adult reconciling

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why the speaker calls his childhood 'a forgotten boredom'.
Analyse the comparison between the speaker's joy at spring and a child who sees adults reconciling.

topics.title: The poet and the poem

concepts.learning_objective: Recall facts about Philip Larkin, the Movement and the volume from which the poem is taken.
Evaluate the poem's quiet, hopeful tone and its short free-verse lines.

topics.title: Haiku

concepts.learning_objective: State the main features of the haiku as a Japanese three-line poem.
Interpret the images and ideas in the haiku 'Cobra', 'Night' and 'Alone'.

topics.title: The speaker's situation and 'self-confession'

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the situation in which the speaker telephones a landlady about renting accommodation.
Explain the irony of the speaker having to 'confess' that he is African.

topics.title: The landlady's response and racial prejudice

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the images that reveal the landlady's refined manner and her silences.
Analyse how the landlady's questions about skin colour expose racial prejudice.

topics.title: The speaker's wit and the ending

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the speaker uses words such as 'sepia', 'brunette' and 'peroxide blonde' humorously.
Evaluate the satirical effect of the speaker's closing question.

topics.title: Language, imagery and vocabulary

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the colour images in the poem and explain their effect.
Interpret wordplay such as 'hide-and-speak' and the use of capital letters.

topics.title: About the poet and the title

concepts.learning_objective: Recall key facts about Wole Soyinka's life, education and achievements.
Evaluate the significance of the title 'Telephone Conversation' and the poet's satirical style.

chapters.title: The World is too Much With Us

topics.title: Materialism and the waste of human powers

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the poet criticises worldly preoccupation with getting and spending.
Interpret the oxymoron 'a sordid boon' and the loss it describes.

topics.title: Nature's beauty and humanity out of tune

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the personified images of the sea and the winds.
Explain what human beings are out of tune with and why it matters.

topics.title: The wish to be a Pagan

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why the poet would rather be a Pagan suckled in a creed outworn.
Recognise the allusions to Proteus and Triton and their purpose.

topics.title: The poet and the sonnet form
topics.ncert_sections: About the Poet; Try This Out

concepts.learning_objective: Analyse the structure, rhyme scheme and turn of this Petrarchan sonnet.
Recall Wordsworth's life, views on poetic language and role in Romanticism.

topics.title: The poet's request for a quill

concepts.learning_objective: Recall how the poet asks the reed for a quill and what the quill stands for.
Interpret the reed's irritated questions and its comparison of the poet to an accountant.

topics.title: Serving the Shahni: the mother tongue Dogri

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the poet presents her mother tongue Dogri as a kind and wealthy Shahni with many servants.
Interpret the reed's act of cutting off its hand as a sign of shared devotion to the language.

topics.title: Poetic devices, tone and theme

concepts.learning_objective: Identify personification and other devices used to give the reed and the language human qualities.
Analyse the sense of urgency and emotional attachment the poet shows towards her mother tongue.

topics.title: About the poet and the Dogri script
topics.ncert_sections: About the Poet; Try This Out

concepts.learning_objective: Recall key facts about Padma Sachdev and her writing in Dogri and Hindi.
Explain how Dogri lost its native script Sharade and which scripts are now used to write it.

topics.title: The hawk at rest: the top of the wood

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the hawk's position and stillness as it sits with closed eyes at the top of the wood.
Explain how the hawk sees the trees, the air, the sun and the earth as existing for its advantage.

topics.title: Physical prowess and 'Creation in my foot'

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the hawk's physical features (hooked head, hooked feet, locked feet, feathers) and their significance.
Interpret the claim that Creation produced the hawk and that it now holds Creation in its foot.

topics.title: Violence, frankness and the allotment of death

concepts.learning_objective: Analyse the images of killing that present the hawk's absolute, unquestioned power.
Explain what the hawk means by 'no sophistry in my body' and 'No arguments assert my right'.

topics.title: Changelessness and the human parallel

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the hawk's claim that nothing has changed and that it will keep things like this.
Evaluate the parallel the poem suggests between the hawk's predatory arrogance and human tyranny.

topics.title: The poet, the monologue form and the language

concepts.learning_objective: Recall key facts about Ted Hughes and the qualities of his animal poems.
Identify the poem as a monologue spoken by the hawk and explain the effect of this form and the title.
Infer the meanings of words such as 'buoyancy' and 'roosting' in the context of the poem.

topics.title: The April evening and the wife's comments

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the relaxed April-evening setting with which the poem opens.
Interpret the wife's comments and the husband's ironic withdrawal from them.

topics.title: The son's demand and the parents' rapport

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the seven-year-old son presents his demand for dinner.
Interpret the parents' unspoken agreement that children must be disciplined.

topics.title: The child's logic and the resolution

concepts.learning_objective: Analyse why the child's argument about hunger seems logical to the father.
Explain how the wife's laughter resolves the scene and unites the family.

topics.title: Poetic craft and the poet

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the use of understatement, irony and asides in the poem.
Explain how the idyllic setting is juxtaposed with ordinary domestic matters.
Recall key facts about the poet Nissim Ezekiel.

topics.title: The Limerick

concepts.learning_objective: State the form and rhyme scheme of a limerick.
Interpret the punch line in the limericks given with the chapter.

topics.title: Homelessness and the lost homeland

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the opening stanza contrasts a crowded city with the refugees' lack of any place.
Interpret the images of the atlas and the yew tree that renews itself while old passports cannot.

topics.title: Bureaucracy and public hostility

concepts.learning_objective: Analyse how the consul and the committee show the cold indifference of official systems.
Interpret the speaker's claim that refugees 'will steal our daily bread' as prejudice against outsiders.

topics.title: Persecution and the contrast with animals and nature

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the historical context of Nazi persecution of German Jews in the poem.
Evaluate how the poodle, cat, fish and birds highlight the refugees' loss of freedom and dignity.

topics.title: Dreams denied and the final threat

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the dream of a building with a thousand doors, none of them the refugees'.
Explain how 'two tickets to Happiness' and the full coaches capture the essence of the poem.
Analyse the menace of the final stanza with ten thousand soldiers searching for the couple.

topics.title: Form, poetic devices and the poet
topics.ncert_sections: About the poet; Try this out

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the ballad and blues form and the role of the refrain in the poem.
Distinguish irony, pathos and sarcasm as used in the poem.
Recall facts about W.H. Auden and explain how the title captures the theme.

topics.title: The father clears the hill

concepts.learning_objective: Recall how the father removed the tenants, the houses and the trees around the family home.
Explain the contrast between the grandmother's belief that trees are sacred and the father's actions.

topics.title: The banyan tree and its felling

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the details the poet gives of the banyan tree's size, roots and age.
Interpret the imagery of slaughter used to describe how the tree was cut down.

topics.title: The tree that grows in dreams

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the significance of the family's move from Baroda to treeless Bombay.
Analyse what the banyan tree that 'grows and seethes' in dreams symbolises.

topics.title: Poet, tone and language

concepts.learning_objective: Recall key facts about Dilip Chitre and the collection the poem comes from.
Identify the critical tone and the meaning of words such as 'scraggy', 'massacred' and 'raw mythology'.

topics.title: Stanza 1: Drowsy numbness and the happy Dryad

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the nightingale's song leaves the poet in a state of painful, drowsy numbness.
Interpret the allusions to hemlock, Lethe and the Dryad in the opening stanza.

topics.title: Stanza 2: The longing for wine

concepts.learning_objective: Analyse why the poet longs for wine as a means of escaping the world.
Identify the meaning of Flora, Provencal and Hippocrene in the stanza.

topics.title: Stanza 3: The weariness, the fever and the fret

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the unpleasant aspects of the human condition the poet wishes to escape.
Explain how the poem shows that beauty and love do not last.

topics.title: Stanza 7: The immortal bird

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the poet brings out the immortality of the nightingale's song.
Interpret the allusion to Ruth and the image of magic casements.

topics.title: Stanza 8: Forlorn, the return to the self

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the word 'forlorn' tosses the poet back from ecstasy to his sole self.
Evaluate how the closing lines bring out the elusive nature of happiness.

topics.title: The poet, form and poetic devices

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the ode form, apostrophe and oxymoron as used in the poem.
Recall facts about John Keats and recognise sensuous imagery of sound, sight and taste.

topics.title: The tigers' complaint and the king's first raid

concepts.learning_objective: Recall why the starving tigers appealed to their king and what they reported about Ajamil's sheep dog.
Interpret the irony in the tiger king's boastful solo raid and its humiliating result.

topics.title: The planned attack and the sheep dog's victory

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the tiger king's second plan of a mass attack led by himself.
Analyse how the poet uses hyperbole to show the sheep dog's speed and alertness.

topics.title: The tiger king's lies and Ajamil's pretence

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the hypocrisy in the tiger king's claim that the tigers came as friends.
Interpret why Ajamil pretended to believe the lies and avoided the sheep dog's eyes.

topics.title: The friendship treaty and the good shepherd

concepts.learning_objective: Recall the dinner, the long-term friendship treaty and the gifts Ajamil gave the tigers.
Evaluate the political wisdom behind Ajamil's decision that even tigers must eat.

topics.title: The poet, the form and the satire

concepts.learning_objective: State key facts about the poet Arun Kolatkar given in the chapter.
Distinguish the poem's literal and figurative levels as fable, allegory and satire.
